habitat.description:
The Bornean orangutan dwells in the ancient dipterocarp rainforests of Borneo, spending nearly all its life in the canopy, moving through a three-dimensional world of branches, lianas, and fruiting trees. These forests, among the oldest on Earth, provide an aerial highway system that orangutans navigate with extraordinary spatial memory.

In the peat swamp forests of the lowlands, orangutans build nightly nests high in the trees, bending and weaving branches into platforms with the skill of practiced architects. The swamp forests, waterlogged and rich in fruit trees, support some of the densest orangutan populations remaining.

Higher on the volcanic slopes of Borneo, montane forests offer a different menu of fruits, bark, and leaves. Here orangutans range more widely, their movements dictated by the irregular fruiting patterns of tropical trees, carrying a mental map of hundreds of food sources across their home ranges.

threats.name: Palm Oil Deforestation
threats.description: Industrial palm oil plantations have destroyed millions of hectares of orangutan habitat, fragmenting populations into isolated patches.

threats.name: Illegal Pet Trade
threats.description: Infant orangutans are captured for the pet trade, with mothers typically killed in the process.

threats.name: Forest Fires
threats.description: Peat fires, often set to clear land for agriculture, devastate orangutan habitat and can burn for months underground.

threats.name: Logging
threats.description: Both legal and illegal timber extraction removes the large fruiting trees that orangutans depend upon for food and nesting.

threats.name: Hunting
threats.description: In some areas orangutans are hunted for bushmeat or killed as crop pests when they venture into plantations.

cultural_significance.cinema: Orangutans feature prominently in documentaries about deforestation, becoming the poster species for the palm oil crisis.
cultural_significance.literature: From Edgar Allan Poe's "Murders in the Rue Morgue" to Terry Pratchett's Librarian, orangutans occupy a unique space in fiction.
cultural_significance.mythology: The name "orangutan" derives from Malay "orang hutan" meaning "person of the forest," reflecting indigenous recognition of their near-human qualities.
cultural_significance.media_presence: David Attenborough's emotional encounters with orangutans have become some of the most shared wildlife television moments.
cultural_significance.cultural_paradox: Our closest relatives in Asia face extinction primarily so that processed foods can contain cheap vegetable oil.

hero_stat: 100 orangutans lost every week due to habitat destruction

interesting_facts.text: Orangutans share approximately 97% of their DNA with humans, making them one of our closest living relatives.
They construct a new sleeping nest every night from branches and leaves, sometimes adding a roof for rain protection.
Orangutans have been observed using tools including sticks to extract honey and leaves as makeshift gloves.
A mother orangutan nurses her young for up to 8 years, one of the longest dependency periods in the animal kingdom.

dayak_forest_people.description: The Dayak peoples of Borneo hold orangutans as forest guardians with near-human intelligence. Traditional stories describe orangutans as humans who retreated into the forest to avoid work or conflict, and some communities maintain taboos against hunting them.

malay_etymology.description: The name "orangutan" derives from Malay "orang hutan" meaning "person of the forest," reflecting the deep cultural recognition of their humanlike qualities. This linguistic connection reveals centuries of coexistence and the perception of orangutans as almost-human forest dwellers.
malay_etymology.source: Rijksen, H.D. & Meijaard, E. (1999). Our Vanishing Relative. Kluwer Academic.

western_science.description: Western scientific encounters with orangutans from the 17th century onward challenged European notions of human uniqueness. Alfred Russel Wallace observed orangutans in Borneo during his development of natural selection theory, describing their tool use and problem-solving with astonishment.

comic_strip.label: In the Wild
comic_strip.title: Canopy World
comic_strip.narrative_text: The Bornean orangutan dwells in ancient dipterocarp rainforests, spending nearly all its life in the canopy. Moving through a three-dimensional world of branches, lianas, and fruiting trees, these great apes navigate with extraordinary spatial memory across one of Earth's oldest forest ecosystems.

comic_strip.label: Under Threat
comic_strip.title: Palm Oil's Price
comic_strip.narrative_text: Industrial palm oil plantations have destroyed millions of hectares of orangutan habitat, fragmenting populations into isolated patches. The global appetite for this cheap vegetable oil drives continuous forest clearing across Borneo and Sumatra.

comic_strip.label: The Human Story
comic_strip.title: Dayak Forest Wisdom
comic_strip.narrative_text: The Dayak peoples of Borneo hold orangutans as forest guardians with near-human intelligence. Traditional stories describe orangutans as humans who retreated into the forest to avoid conflict, and some communities maintain taboos against hunting them.

comic_strip.label: Fighting Back
comic_strip.title: Survival Foundation
comic_strip.narrative_text: The Borneo Orangutan Survival Foundation rescues displaced and orphaned orangutans, rehabilitating them for release back into protected forests. Together with HUTAN-KOCP and the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil, these programs work to secure remaining habitat.

comic_strip.label: The Future
comic_strip.title: Critically Endangered
comic_strip.narrative_text: With approximately 104,700 individuals remaining and populations still decreasing, the Bornean orangutan is Critically Endangered. At current rates of habitat loss, scientists estimate significant further decline without immediate and sustained intervention.
